ai.definition: Synthetic Carbon Scrubbers are engineered ecosystems that utilize a consortium of genetically modified algae and bacteria to efficiently capture atmospheric CO2. These systems are designed to operate in urban settings, where they can be integrated into infrastructure like building facades or vertical gardens.
ai.howItWorks: The system works by introducing modified RuBisCO enzymes into the algae-bacteria consortia, which enhances their ability to fix carbon dioxide more efficiently than natural counterparts. This modification allows for faster and higher rates of CO2 capture from the surrounding air, with the captured CO2 being used in various applications such as biofuels or chemical feedstocks.
ai.problemSolved: These scrubbers address the challenge of reducing atmospheric CO2 levels in urban areas where traditional methods like afforestation are less feasible due to space constraints and other limitations. They offer a scalable solution for carbon capture that can be deployed in densely populated regions.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves genetic modification of algae and bacteria strains, followed by their cultivation in controlled environments such as bioreactors or engineered structures. The integration into urban infrastructure requires careful design to ensure structural integrity and environmental compatibility.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes site selection, structural engineering for integration with existing buildings, installation of bioreactor systems, and the introduction and maintenance of the modified algae-bacteria consortia. Regular monitoring is required to optimize performance and ensure long-term viability.
ai.costDrivers: Key cost drivers include genetic modification technologies, initial setup costs for bioreactors or cultivation structures, ongoing operational costs such as energy for lighting and temperature control in urban environments, and regular maintenance of the systems.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is currently at an early stage of development with significant potential for future commercialization. Continued R&D is needed to refine efficiency and scalability before broader deployment can occur.
ai.regulation: There are currently no specific regulations governing synthetic carbon scrubbers, but environmental and safety standards will likely be required as the technology advances towards commercial use. Regulations related to genetic modification of organisms may also apply.
ai.risks: Potential risks include unintended ecological impacts from modified organisms escaping into natural environments, concerns over biosecurity if genetically engineered microorganisms are used, and challenges in ensuring long-term stability and performance of the systems in urban settings.
ai.profitability: Profitability is currently speculative given the early stage of development. However, successful commercialization could lead to significant financial benefits through carbon credits or by selling captured CO2 for various industrial applications.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may focus on improving the efficiency and scalability of the systems, expanding their application in different urban environments, and addressing potential regulatory challenges associated with genetic modification technologies.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds to thousands of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and other purification processes required for genetic modifications.

glossary.def: Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase, an enzyme involved in the first step of carbon fixation in photosynthesis.
A device used to cultivate microorganisms under controlled conditions for various applications such as biotechnology and environmental remediation.

subsystems.name: Engineered enzymes
subsystems.role: speed up carbon fixation beyond natural limits.

subsystems.name: Microbial consortium
subsystems.role: a cooperative community of algae and bacteria that captures CO2 and grows reliably.

subsystems.name: Bioreactor
subsystems.role: contains the culture, supplies light and CO2, and controls conditions.
parts: transparent tubes or panels (closed photobioreactor) or shallow raceway ponds

subsystems.name: CO2 delivery
subsystems.role: brings concentrated CO2 from a flue gas or air-capture source into the culture.

subsystems.name: Harvesting and processing
subsystems.role: separates biomass from water and converts it into useful products.
parts: conversion units for fuels, chemicals or fertiliser

buildSteps.title: Engineer the enzymes
buildSteps.detail: Use directed evolution or rational design to create RuBisCO variants with faster turnover and less oxygen inhibition, and engineer carboxysome shells to concentrate CO2 around the enzyme.

buildSteps.title: Modify the microbes
buildSteps.detail: Edit the genomes of algae and bacteria with CRISPR and other tools to boost CO2 uptake, growth rate and the exchange of nutrients between partners.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the consortium
buildSteps.detail: Co-culture selected strains in the lab and select combinations that remain stable and productive over many generations.

buildSteps.title: Build the bioreactor
buildSteps.detail: Construct closed photobioreactors or open raceway ponds with controlled light, mixing, temperature and pH, sized for the intended CO2 source.

buildSteps.title: Start and operate the culture
buildSteps.detail: Inoculate with the consortium, supply CO2, water and nutrients, and maintain conditions so the culture captures carbon at a high rate.

buildSteps.title: Harvest and process biomass
buildSteps.detail: Separate the grown biomass from water, dry it, and convert it into products such as biofuels, bioplastics or soil amendments.

buildSteps.title: Recycle water and nutrients
buildSteps.detail: Recover and reuse the growth medium to reduce cost and environmental impact.

prerequisites.why: needed to modify RuBisCO, carboxysomes and microbial metabolism.
the enzyme is slow and oxygen-sensitive, and engineering it without breaking the cell is still an active research problem.
closed systems have been built at pilot scale, but cost, light delivery and contamination remain challenges.
capturing CO2 from flue gas is established, but direct air capture is energy-intensive and costly.

pathway.milestone: lab-scale demonstration of engineered enzymes and consortia with improved carbon fixation rates
pathway.unlocks: proof that the biological parts can work together.

pathway.milestone: pilot-scale photobioreactors coupled to an industrial CO2 source, testing stability and productivity over months
pathway.unlocks: real-world data on cost, contamination and yield.

pathway.milestone: commercial modules for point-source capture that produce high-value products
pathway.unlocks: a business case for deployment at factories and power plants.

pathway.milestone: deployment for direct air capture if energy and material costs fall
pathway.unlocks: a route to negative emissions at climate-relevant scale.
